coders.commentText: Focusable element is not in keyboard tab order

cases.aspectTitle: Scripted elements that look like links/buttons but expose a generic role or none (F42)
cases.scenario: BOUNDARY/PASS — Nonprofit donation page (Riverbank Trust) whose amount chooser ($25/$50/$100/Other) and 'Continue' action are built from the SAME styled <div> pill building blocks as the failing cases (rounded, filled-when-selected, pointer cursor), but each emulated control correctly EXPOSES the role it presents: role=radiogroup with role=radio children (aria-checked, roving tabindex, arrow-key nav) and role=button with tabindex+keydown.
cases.mechanism: The amount pills are <div role="radio" aria-checked> inside <div role="radiogroup" aria-labelledby> and 'Continue' is <div role="button" tabindex="0">; verified as accessibility role 'radio' with name '$25' (and the strip as a radio group) and focusable=true, so the control and selection relationships conveyed by the styling ARE programmatically determinable — not an F42 failure, since F42 fails only when the exposed role is generic/absent/wrong.

cases.aspectTitle: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
cases.scenario:
Municipal building-permit 'Scope' section: two stacked yes/no questions — 'Will the work change the building's footprint?' (name=footprint) and 'Is the property in a flood-hazard zone?' (name=flood). Each question is a styled

; each radio pair is labelled Yes/No via
cases.mechanism: All four radios have valid Yes/No accessible names (e086e5 passes). A screen-reader user navigating by form control lands on 'Yes, radio button, 1 of 2' with no programmatic context about which question it answers; both groups announce the same Yes/No and the questions are unassociated paragraphs. Identical option labels across two ungrouped sets create ambiguous group membership — the disambiguator (the stacked prose question) never reaches the accessibility tree.

cases.aspectTitle: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
cases.scenario: Arabic (lang=ar, dir=rtl) Health-Ministry new-patient form: a split date-of-birth control with three inputs for اليوم/الشهر/السنة (Day/Month/Year) under a single styled <div> heading تاريخ الميلاد (Date of birth). Each input is named via title='يوم'/'شهر'/'سنة', so no input is unnamed, but there is no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=group+aria-labelledby tying the three inputs to the one question they jointly answer; RTL adds a visual-vs-source ordering wrinkle.
cases.mechanism: Each date input has a non-empty accessible name from title (e086e5 passes). AT encounters three independent fields ('Year, edit text', 'Month...', 'Day...') with no announcement that they compose a single Date of birth value; the unifying question is an unassociated <div> never spoken on entry. The sub-names are ambiguous out of context ('Year' of what?). TT 5.C requires the controls be programmatically associated with their shared question.

cases.aspectTitle: Layout tables that falsely assert data-table relationships: th, caption, scope, or summary on a positioning-only table (F46)
cases.scenario: A weekly typography newsletter (The Proof Sheet, Issue 47) is built from deeply nested HTML-email layout tables. Every layout table is correctly role="presentation" EXCEPT the masthead 'header band', which was copied from a data-table block in the ESP snippet library and still carries a <th scope="col">The Proof Sheet</th> and has no presentation role — so that single band re-enters the accessibility tree as a data table whose column header is 'The Proof Sheet'.
cases.mechanism: Because role="presentation" is absent on the header band AND it contains a <th>, AT re-exposes that band as a data table: 'table, 1 column', with 'The Proof Sheet' announced as the column header for the issue-line cell beneath it — a fabricated relationship (it is just a masthead). The surrounding presentational tables read normally, so the experience is one jarring 'table' interruption asserting structure that does not exist. F46 names a <th> in a layout table as a failure; TT 14.C requires layout tables to carry no header structure (or to be role=presentation).

coders.commentText: Different issue, it should be for 3.2.1 which is on focus

cases.aspectTitle: Applicability gate — author-controlled tooltip vs. user-agent title= tooltip (and modal-dialog carve-out)
cases.scenario: Meridian Bank wire-transfer form: focusing the high-risk Amount field opens a modal security step-up dialog (role='dialog' aria-modal='true') that dims the page, moves keyboard focus to its confirm button, traps Tab, and is dismissed via Escape/Cancel. Superficially this is content appearing on focus (the 1.4.13 trigger pattern), but modal dialogs are explicitly out of scope — the correct disposition is NOT-APPLICABLE to 1.4.13 (evaluate under 3.2.1 On Focus). This is the N/A modal carve-out anchor.
cases.mechanism: The focus-triggered content is a modal: it takes keyboard focus (focus moved into the dialog), traps it, dims the page, and must be acknowledged. The 1.4.13 modal exclusion states modals must take keyboard focus and thus should not appear on hover/focus in the transient sense the SC governs, routing such content to 3.2.1 On Focus. So 1.4.13 does not apply. Verified with Puppeteer: dialog has aria-modal='true'; focusing #amount sets backdrop data-open='true' and moves document.activeElement to dlg-confirm (focus enters the dialog) — confirming modal behavior (screenshot showed the dimmed page + modal).

coders.commentText: The audit incorrectly applies the 3:1 contrast exception for inline links, failing to enforce the requirement for redundant structural cues (like underlines) as defined by our strict 1.4.1 testing parameters.

cases.aspectTitle: Inline links distinguished from body text by hue alone (no underline/weight/lightness), incl. hover/focus-only cues that don't rescue
cases.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (PASS / escape-hatch boundary). Nonprofit 'Where your gift goes' donation/impact page reproducing the literal G183 example: inline links medium-light blue #3366CC, no underline, on black #000000 body over white. A bonus :hover/:focus underline is added but is not what carries conformance.
cases.mechanism: Link #3366CC vs black body text is 3.91:1 lightness contrast, at/above the 3:1 escape hatch, so links are distinguishable by lightness (not hue alone) even with no color perception or in grayscale. Link-vs-white-bg is 5.37:1, so 1.4.3 also passes. The page does not depend on the hover/focus underline.

coders.commentText: It lacks a true non-color structural fallback, and relying on the 3:1 contrast escape hatch does not meet our requirement for redundant visual cues

cases.aspectTitle: Required form fields indicated by color alone, with self-referential or absent text instruction
cases.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE via the lightness escape hatch. Developer-console 'Create API key' form. Required labels are green (#2e8b2e), optional labels charcoal (#222). No '(required)' text — but the two colours differ in BOTH hue and lightness: their inter-colour contrast is ~3.67:1 (>=3:1), green-on-white is 4.33:1 and charcoal-on-white 15.9:1. The required/optional distinction survives greyscale as a light-vs-dark difference. Should PASS via the escape hatch.
cases.mechanism: The two label colours differ in lightness by a contrast ratio >=3:1, which the 1.4.1 Understanding note counts as an additional visual distinction, so the distinction is not hue-only; passes 1.4.1 even with no text cue (aria-required absence is a separate 1.3.1/3.3.2 matter, not 1.4.1).

coders.commentText: The ordering is a bit inconsistent with the layout of the page. It has an ordering that goes down and up and down the page, which is inconsistent/that does not preserve meaning. Meaning that 2.4.3 is not met.

cases.aspectTitle: Positive tabindex creates a tab order that does not preserve meaning (F44), with the meaning-judgment a human must make
cases.scenario: BOUNDARY counter-example: an engineering-blog post footer with a row of five social-share buttons (X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Email, Copy link) carrying SCRAMBLED positive tabindex 3,1,4,2,5. Despite positive tabindex present AND in a scrambled order, the five actions are mutually independent so their order carries no meaning - the canonical 'row of social-media icons' Does-Not-Apply example.
cases.mechanism: tabindex scrambles the share-button order (verified traversal: Facebook->Email->X->LinkedIn->Copy link), but each button is a complete independent action with no sequence/dependency, and the rest of the page (article + related links, no tabindex) tabs in normal DOM order. The navigation sequence does not affect meaning or operability, so SC 2.4.3 does not apply.

cases.aspectTitle: A specific, well-formed link name that contradicts its actual on-page destination (deceptive but descriptive name)
cases.scenario: SaaS pricing page with three tier cards (Basic free, Pro, Enterprise) and three on-page sign-up sections (#basic-signup, #pro-signup, #enterprise-checkout). The Basic card's CTA reads 'Basic plan — $0/mo: Get started free' but its href is '#enterprise-checkout', the paid Enterprise purchase flow ($1,200/mo, annual contract). Honest target is #basic-signup.
cases.mechanism: The free-plan CTA's specific name 'Basic plan — $0/mo: Get started free' resolves to '#enterprise-checkout' — the paid Enterprise checkout section — instead of '#basic-signup'; the link's name describes a free signup while its actual destination is a high-commitment paid purchase flow, so the name does not describe the real purpose.

cases.aspectTitle: Error is conveyed via an icon/image that HAS a text alternative, but the alt/name misstates, genericises, or mislocates the error
cases.scenario: Workforce SaaS password reset; the user supplied a 7-char password (policy requires 10) so the field is filled-but-too-short, yet the error icon emitted by a validation-plugin template carries alt="This field is required" — the wrong cause.
cases.mechanism: The icon exposes role=img name="This field is required" (CDP-confirmed), tied to the field via aria-errormessage. The field is not empty (value summer7); the announced cause (required/omitted) contradicts the true error (outside required values — too short), so the user re-types content that is already present and never learns the real rule.

cases.aspectTitle: Error is signalled ONLY by visual styling (red border / colour / icon glyph) with no error meaning in text anywhere on the page
cases.scenario: Bank reset-password screen redisplayed after rejecting a reused password; the field shows a red outline + a red CSS ::before key glyph and carries aria-invalid='true', but emits NO error text, aria-errormessage, or aria-describedby — nothing in words states what is wrong or why.
cases.mechanism: aria-invalid='true' conveys only THAT the field is invalid, not WHAT the error is; SC 3.3.1 requires the error be described in text. There is no message and no aria-errormessage/aria-describedby to read, and the red ::before key is CSS generated content outside the accessibility tree, so a non-visual user learns at most 'invalid' with no reason.

cases.aspectTitle: Genuine data tables whose header/structure semantics are absent or stripped: all-<td> tables, and real data tables with role=presentation (F91, F92)
cases.scenario: An order-confirmation email containing TWO tables: (A) a layout table (greeting + order badge) correctly given role='presentation' with no headers, and (B) a genuine order line-items data table correctly built with <caption>, <th scope='col'>, and <th scope='row'>. Both choices are correct. Boundary PASS variant that sharpens the layout-vs-data distinction.
cases.mechanism: Correct retention vs. correct suppression: the layout table's role=presentation correctly removes unneeded table semantics (it reads sensibly in source order), while the data table correctly keeps caption + scope so every cell ('$9.00') announces its column header ('Unit price') and row header ('Reusable filter (size 02)'). No information or relationship is lost (TT 14.A/14.B pass for the data table; 14.C passes for the layout table).

cases.aspectTitle: Emphasis or special-status meaning conveyed only by visual text variation, with no markup or text equivalent (G117, H49)
cases.scenario: BOUNDARY/PASS variant: a product maintenance guide where the one safety-critical step (shut off water before opening housing) is visually emphasised bold+larger — the same risky pattern — BUT uses <strong> markup (H49) AND begins with the literal word 'Important:' in text (G117), so the special status is both programmatically determinable and available in text.
cases.mechanism: The status is conveyed by the word 'Important:' (text equivalent per G117) AND by the <strong> element (programmatically-determinable strong importance per H49), so a screen-reader/braille user gets the warning regardless of styling; the larger font-size is now redundant decoration. Presentation PLUS a text/markup equivalent — 1.3.1 met.

cases.aspectTitle: Visual-only headings: text styled to look like a heading but marked up as plain p/div/span (F2)
cases.scenario: BOUNDARY PASS: coffee-roastery 'Our Story' page where the giant brand tagline 'Slow coffee, made by hand.' and a centered italic pull-quote 'The best cup I've had in this city.' are large/bold but correctly NOT headings (decorative statement + excerpt), while the three genuine section headings ('Where we started', 'How we roast', 'Visit the bar') are exposed via role=heading aria-level=2 (design-system-without-native-h* persona).
cases.mechanism: The three role=heading paragraphs expose as heading level 2 and each precedes the section it titles; the tagline exposes as paragraph and the pull-quote as blockquote (read in flow, not announced as headings). Live AX returned exactly the three real section headings and neither the tagline nor the pull-quote — every visual heading is programmatically determinable AND no non-heading is falsely a heading (TT 10.B both directions).

cases.aspectTitle: Visually apparent lists not programmatically identified as lists (or as the wrong type / lost nesting)
cases.scenario: PASS boundary: a parks 'Trail Conditions' page that does it correctly — three trailheads mentioned as a comma-separated inline run inside a sentence (correctly NOT a list), a genuinely ordered 'Before you hike' procedure coded as <ol>, and a genuinely term/description marker glossary coded as <dl>/<dt>/<dd>.
cases.mechanism: Every visually apparent list is programmatically a list of the correct type: the <ol> exposes ordered/positional list semantics matching the visible numbered steps, the <dl> exposes a description-list group pairing each dt term with its dd, and the comma-separated trailheads are normal sentence prose with no visual list to mismatch — so no list markup is owed (TT 10.D note).

cases.aspectTitle: Dismissible Method 1 — pop-up obscures meaningful content (beyond the white-space / decorative exception)
cases.scenario: Restaurant menu: a dish allergen tooltip opens into an empty menu band occupied only by a large decorative olive-branch SVG flourish (aria-hidden, no information), with no Esc dismiss. Overlap is with purely decorative content — PASS by the decorative carve-out.
cases.mechanism: The tooltip (role=tooltip) overlaps only svg.flourish (aria-hidden, conveys nothing) and is verified clear of every dish name/description/price/heading. Because the only covered thing is 'a background graphic which provides no information,' Method 1's exception applies and the missing dismiss mechanism is acceptable.

cases.aspectTitle: Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)
cases.scenario:
Charity grant-spending page: one sentence (one

) offers the SAME four-row dataset in three takeaway formats, each behind an identical link named 'Download this data' — a PDF, an XLSX and a CSV delivered via self-contained data: URIs. Identical name, identical same-DOM-node context, but the destinations are equivalent (same data, different format). PASS boundary control where the discriminator is purpose-equivalence.
cases.mechanism: Three <a download> with identical accessible name 'Download this data' in one paragraph resolve to three encodings (PDF/XLSX/CSV) of one identical dataset (the CSV data: URI literally encodes the same Food/Fuel/Children/Rent figures shown in the table). Per fd3a94's expectation, links sharing name+context PASS when they resolve to equivalent resources; 'same data, different file format' is the canonical equivalence (mirrored by the Understanding's HTML/PDF/mp3 'list of book titles' example). Every user gets the same content from any link, so each link's purpose — obtain this dataset — is determinable.
cases.primarySelector: p > a[download$=".pdf"], p > a[download$=".xlsx"], p > a[download$=".csv"]

cases.aspectTitle: Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)
cases.scenario: Volunteer-run tech conference page (negative control): one paragraph contains two inline links both named 'contact us' in the same sentence-pair, one framed around accessibility needs and one around invoices/VAT receipts. Both point to the SAME #contact section — one shared organiser inbox handling every request (verified: 2 occurrences, 1 unique destination). Looks like the failing duplicate-name pattern but is benign because the destination is one and the same.
cases.mechanism: Two <a href="#contact"> with identical accessible name 'contact us' and identical context both resolve to the SAME in-page target (one <h2 id="contact"> shared-inbox section). Per fd3a94 this PASSES because 'both links resolve to the same resource' — the strongest equivalence. The surrounding clauses describe two topics (access vs finance) but both are served by one team at one address, so whichever link the user picks, the purpose (reach the organisers) is satisfied identically and no user is misled.

cases.aspectTitle: Generic/boilerplate link text with a non-empty name but no purpose, and no context that rescues it (G91/H30 substantive failure)
cases.scenario: SaaS pricing page: a paragraph reads '...for full pricing details, click here.' where the generic phrase 'click here' is the link but the purpose words ('full pricing details') precede it in the SAME sentence — the boundary near-PASS that is identical boilerplate to a failing page, rescued only by its enclosing sentence (G53).
cases.mechanism: The link's same-sentence programmatically determined context names the destination's purpose ('full pricing details') BEFORE the generic phrase, so a screen-reader user reading the paragraph hears the purpose first and can identify the link without leaving it; 2.4.4 is satisfied by link text combined with programmatic context per technique G53.

cases.aspectTitle: Generic/boilerplate link text with a non-empty name but no purpose, and no context that rescues it (G91/H30 substantive failure)
cases.scenario: Public-health dashboard: a bar chart of childhood MMR coverage with a <figcaption> ending in a 'learn more' link. The caption sentence names the destination subject ('the methodology and clinic-level breakdown behind this 2025 dip in MMR coverage') immediately before the generic phrase, and the link lives INSIDE the figcaption — the hardest borderline PASS.
cases.mechanism: The link is a descendant of the <figcaption>, which is the link's containing block (and the figure's accessible name via aria-labelledby); the caption sentence names the subject BEFORE 'learn more', so a screen-reader user reading the caption hears the purpose first and can identify the link in context (2.4.4 same-block rule + G53). Accessible name confirmed as 'learn more' via AX tree.

cases.aspectTitle: Image/icon/SVG-only links with a non-empty name that misdescribes or fails to convey the rendered glyph's purpose (F89 semantic-mismatch variant)
cases.scenario: Boundary PASS control: a municipal transit (Route 12 schedule) utility bar of three icon-only links — house (aria-label="Metro Transit home"), printer (aria-label="Print this schedule"), telephone (aria-label="Call rider services: 311", a tel: link). Each has a non-empty name AND the name correctly describes the rendered glyph and the link's purpose, so the page satisfies 2.4.4.
cases.mechanism: Each <a> is role=link with a non-empty accessible name from aria-label that matches its glyph and destination (confirmed via CDP: "Metro Transit home" / "Print this schedule" / "Call rider services: 311"; SVGs aria-hidden). A screen-reader user can determine each link's purpose from the link text alone. Both the name-presence floor (c487ae/F89) and the descriptive limb of 2.4.4 are met.

cases.aspectTitle: Sufficiency of preceding-heading / list-grouping context as the purpose carrier (H80 judgment, including when the heading is NOT the link's context)
cases.scenario: A borough council publications page. Each document (Annual Report 2023-2024, Local Plan Review, Council Tax Booklet) is offered in three formats; a real <h2> names the document and the three short format links (HTML/PDF/RTF) sit in the SAME paragraph directly beneath it (H80 Example 2 done correctly). The deliberate PASS boundary variant.
cases.mechanism: For each format link the immediately preceding heading is the document title; link text combined with that heading conveys the purpose ('Annual Report 2023-2024, PDF format'). The heading is genuinely the link's grouping heading and the links + their disambiguating context are within one tightly-scoped <article>, satisfying the H80 test. Identical short format words ('PDF') resolve to different unambiguous purposes because they fall under different headings.

cases.aspectTitle: Error is conveyed via an icon/image that HAS a text alternative, but the alt/name misstates, genericises, or mislocates the error
cases.scenario: CONTROL (passes): government heating-assistance application; the email carla.mendes#state.gov uses # instead of @ and the error icon carries a correct, specific alt="Email address must contain an @ symbol — for example, name@example.com", echoed by a linked error summary.
cases.mechanism: The icon exposes role=img with the full descriptive accessible name (CDP-confirmed) via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears the field identified and the actual error (missing @) described in a text alternative, with a matching summary — satisfying the SC's "in text or a text alternative" limb.

cases.aspectTitle: Post-submit page suppresses the error: form silently re-displayed (or shows a neutral/success banner) after a real validation failure — trigger-and-observe failure of NO indicator
cases.scenario: CONTROL (discrimination boundary): the same Riverbend Library membership flow as case-01, but the genuine SUCCESS result after VALID input (Age 34, a real email). The server accepted the data and rendered a true confirmation — a read-only summary of the accepted values, a real membership number (RVB-2026-08831), and next steps — with no editable form re-displayed and legitimately no error message. Must be judged passed while case-01..05 are failed.
cases.mechanism: 3.3.1 applies only when an input error is automatically detected; here none was — the submission succeeded — so the absence of an error message is correct, required behaviour (ACT Passed Example 3). The page-state cues all point to genuine success: valid accepted values, a real reference number, no editable form to re-submit, and honest success copy conveyed in text. This is the legitimate counterpart that separates a benign result page from a suppressed-failure page.

cases.aspectTitle: Non-empty alt that is not actually an alternative: filename, placeholder, or auto-generated label (F30)
cases.scenario: PASS control: a photo-essay 'photo of the day' showing the same kind of protest scene as case-01, but with a genuine descriptive alt='Crowd marching past the domed City Hall building, holding banners reading Fair fares and No hike'.
cases.mechanism: The image's accessible name is a full scene description that can substitute for the photo (G94): removing the image and leaving the alt loses no essential information, so the equivalence/descriptiveness facet passes alongside presence.

cases.aspectTitle: Complex image (chart/diagram/map) has a plausible alt/long description that drops information the image conveys (F67)
cases.scenario: Finance dashboard with a four-bar quarterly-revenue chart showing three quarters of growth then a sharp red-highlighted Q4 collapse annotated '↓ port strike'. The aria-describedby caption recites the four dollar figures but never states the trend, which bar is the outlier, or the on-chart cause.
cases.mechanism: F67/G92: the chart has aria-label + aria-describedby (both present), but the description gives only isolated data points and drops the trend (rise then collapse), the outlier (Q4, drawn red), and the annotated cause — so substituting the description for the image loses the chart's actual message.

cases.aspectTitle: Alt literally describes the image but is wrong for the image's purpose-in-context (link target or control function)
cases.scenario: News aggregator grid: a newspaper front-page thumbnail is the sole content of a link to the publication's homepage, but its alt accurately describes the cover PHOTO ('Front page photo of a flooded town square under grey skies') instead of naming the publication. A correctly-labelled card (alt='The Harbor Gazette') is included for contrast.
cases.mechanism: Because the is the only content of the , the image alt becomes the link's accessible name. The link to The Riverside Courier is therefore named for the cover photograph, not the publication, so the alternative does not serve the link's purpose-in-context (G94/H30 linked-thumbnail rule).

cases.aspectTitle: Information conveyed exclusively by a CSS background-image (no img element, no DOM text equivalent)
cases.scenario: Building-society loan card whose headline rate '19.3% APR Typical Variable' lives only as pixels in a stylesheet background-image SVG; the visible DOM prose says only 'Where else would you find a better interest rate?' (verbatim F3 example 1).
cases.mechanism: The load-bearing price (19.3% APR Typical Variable) is rendered exclusively by `p#bestinterest { background-image: url(svg) }`. A CSS background image generates no accessibility-tree node and cannot carry a text alternative, so a screen-reader user hears the unanswered question and never learns the rate; forced-colors/hide-backgrounds drops it for sighted users too.

coders.commentText: False positive, the rationale itself explicitly proves the component is compliant, rendering the failure classification invalid

cases.aspectTitle: Information conveyed exclusively by a CSS background-image (no img element, no DOM text equivalent)
cases.scenario: PASS control: order-tracking timeline using the SAME CSS background-image status-badge carrier as the failing pages, but the meaning of every badge ('Order confirmed', 'Out for delivery', 'Delivered') is also written as real adjacent text and the badges are aria-hidden, so the image is redundant.
cases.mechanism: `.badge.done/.truck/.wait` are aria-hidden background-image glyphs; the equivalent status is a real text node in the sibling `.step .status` in the same logical order. A screen-reader user hears every status as text once, cleanly; hide-backgrounds/forced-colors loses nothing. The background images are decorative reinforcements of text, satisfying F3 step 2 / TT 7.C.

cases.aspectTitle: A genuinely informative/functional image marked decorative (alt="" / role=presentation) so AT cannot reach it
cases.scenario: Marketplace listing whose 'Verified seller' green-check badge — the only per-listing signal that this seller passed identity verification — is an inline SVG suppressed from AT via role=presentation + aria-hidden. Unverified sellers render the same row without the check, so the badge's presence is the data; no text states this seller is verified.
cases.mechanism: Informative trust badge declared decorative: the wrapper span carries role=presentation and the SVG aria-hidden=true, so the verification fact is pruned from the accessibility tree though it is the sole per-listing carrier (Trusted Tester 7.B condition 1 fails; F38/F39 inverted).

cases.aspectTitle: Valid structural elements asserting relationships that do not exist: heading/blockquote/fieldset used for visual effect (F43)
cases.scenario: Long-form news article: the byline ("By Marguerite Adler and Tomas Vance") is marked up as <h3> and the dateline as <h4>, between the <h1> title and the real <h2> sections, purely to size them. The byline/date begin no section, fabricating a heading outline (h1 > h3 > h4 > h2) that asserts subsection relationships absent from the content.
cases.mechanism: Screen-reader heading navigation (H key / rotor) announces the byline as a level-3 section and the dateline as a level-4 subsection nested under the title; landing on each, the user finds only author names / a date — no section. Headings assert sectioning relationships (F43) that do not exist; the real first section 'Abstract' is announced after a spurious h3/h4, corrupting the outline.

cases.aspectTitle: Valid structural elements asserting relationships that do not exist: heading/blockquote/fieldset used for visual effect (F43)
cases.scenario: Food-blog recipe: under the real <h2> 'Ingredients', each of six ingredient lines ('2 cups all-purpose flour' …) is marked up as its own <h5> to render in a uniform bold serif. Each ingredient is a list item, not a section heading, so six sibling <h5> elements fabricate subsections that reflect no section structure (and the visually apparent list is also not coded as a list).
cases.mechanism: Pulling up the headings list, a screen-reader user hears each ingredient announced as a heading-level-5 section nested under 'Ingredients', asserting that each ingredient introduces a subsection — a relationship that does not exist; the ingredients are peers in one list. Six non-headings between two real sections make the heading rotor useless and misrepresent flat list items as a hierarchy (F43; also TT 10.D list-not-marked-up).

coders.commentText: This is a false positive because the $3.0M quota line and textual data labels provide sufficient non-color visual cues, rendering the F13 rationale invalid.

cases.aspectTitle: Informational image/chart HAS a text alternative, but the alt restates the color RULE instead of resolving the color-encoded fact
cases.scenario: SaaS sales-analytics board-pack panel: a bar-chart (inline-SVG data: URI) of four reps' annual sales vs a $3.0M quota. Fred ($2.6M) and Bob ($2.2M) are drawn red (below quota), Mary/Andrew green. The alt lists all four figures and states 'the bars shown in red indicate sales below the yearly quota' but never names Fred and Bob. Canonical F13 case.
cases.mechanism: F13 — alt restates the colour rule ('red = below quota') and all data values but omits the resolved fact (which reps are below quota); below-quota membership exists only as the red fill of the 2nd and 3rd bars in a raster image, reaching neither AT nor colour-blind sighted users.
cases.primarySelector: figure img[alt^="Bar chart of FY24 annual sales"]

cases.aspectTitle: Inline links distinguished from body text by hue alone (no underline/weight/lightness), incl. hover/focus-only cues that don't rescue
cases.scenario: Sourdough-focaccia recipe blog using the literal F73 stylesheet pattern: a:link/a:visited/a:active have text-decoration:none (resting green #1f6f43), and only a:hover (plus a:active) add an underline and red color. No :focus rule, so keyboard users also get color-only at rest.
cases.mechanism: In the resting state the only link-vs-text difference is hue (green vs near-black #2b2b2b) at 2.30:1 lightness, below 3:1. The underline/red cue exists in CSS and fires on mouseover but appears only on :hover/:active, and F73/G183 judge conformance before focus or pointing, so the hover-only cue does not rescue the color-only resting state.

cases.aspectTitle: Required form fields indicated by color alone, with self-referential or absent text instruction
cases.scenario: Job-application form (ATS / job board). Required fields are flagged ONLY by a 3px red left-border on the input/select control itself (.field--required → border-left:3px solid #d32f2f); optional fields keep a plain grey border. cases.aspectTitle: Focus order interleaves between two semantically distinct sections/groups (the canonical Understanding form failure)
cases.scenario: Round-trip flight search (SkyHop) with two vertically stacked, headed panels — Outbound flight (From, To, Depart date, Passengers) above Return flight (From, To, Return date, Cabin). The DOM emits the eight fields in alternating legs (outbound-From, return-From, outbound-To, return-To, ...) and CSS grid routes each field back into its panel, so with no tabindex keyboard focus bounces between the outbound and return legs on every Tab while a sighted user sees two clean stacked cards.
cases.mechanism: Two semantic groups (the outbound and return trip legs) are interleaved by raw source order, so focus alternates between the two stacked panels instead of completing one leg before the other. For a round trip the legs are conceptually sequential (go, then return); interleaving them mid-entry forces the user to specify the return origin before finishing the outbound leg and makes it easy to type a return city into an outbound field, corrupting the model of which leg is being edited.

(3.3.1/4.1.2 gaps remain but are out of scope.)

cases.aspectTitle: Informational image/chart HAS a text alternative, but the alt restates the color RULE instead of resolving the color-encoded fact
cases.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE / PASS boundary: the same sales bar chart as case-01 (four reps vs a $3.0M quota, below-quota bars red), but as an inline SVG whose aria-label RESOLVES the fact ('Fred and Bob are the two who fell below the quota; Mary and Andrew met it'). The caption repeats it in bold visible text, a data table repeats it, and the below-quota bars carry non-colour cues (a '▼ below quota' tag and a hatch pattern), making colour redundant.
cases.mechanism: Satisfies G14 — the colour-encoded fact (who is below quota) is conveyed in text (accessible name, caption, table) and via non-colour visible cues (▼ tag, hatch), so no user must perceive red. The inverse of F13; colour is a redundant enhancement, exactly what WCAG permits.

cases.aspectTitle: Inline links distinguished from body text by hue alone (no underline/weight/lightness), incl. hover/focus-only cues that don't rescue
cases.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (INAPPLICABLE / non-applicability boundary). Bank Acceptable Use Policy. Three inline clause hyperlinks (.inline-ref) are styled identical to neighboring static text: same color #202124, same weight, no underline, no hover/focus change. A normal blue underlined footer link is a distractor.
cases.mechanism: Link color equals body color (1.00:1), so there is NO color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink and adjacent static text for anyone — full-color, color-blind, or grayscale. 1.4.1 protects information conveyed by color; here color conveys nothing about the link, so a color-blind user is at no disadvantage. Programmatic link-discoverability for AT is governed by 1.3.1/4.1.2, not 1.4.1.

cases.aspectTitle: Required form fields indicated by color alone, with self-referential or absent text instruction
cases.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE. University course-registration form. Required fields are red AND every required label contains the explicit text cue '(required)' (e.g. 'Student ID (required)'), backed by an at-top legend 'Required fields are shown in red and marked with (required)', plus aria-required='true'. Colour is redundant, not the sole means — implements G205 correctly. Should PASS.
cases.mechanism: G205 satisfied: a visible non-colour textual cue ('(required)') identifies every required field, so use-of-colour is redundant and the required/optional distinction survives greyscale, colour-vision deficiency, and screen-reader announcement; meets 1.4.1.

cases.aspectTitle: Scoping boundary cases: 3:1-lightness pass, pure-color reliance fails regardless of contrast, non-applicability, and visited-link exemption
cases.scenario: Government council cookie-and-tracking policy whose inline links are styled to look exactly like the surrounding static text (inherited colour, no underline at rest). Because colour is not used to distinguish the link from static text at all, SC 1.4.1 does not apply — there is no use-of-colour failure (NOT-APPLICABLE / pass).
cases.mechanism: For 1.4.1 the question is whether colour conveys information. The inline links inherit the body colour (#222) identical to the adjacent static text, so colour is not being used to distinguish the actionable link from the static text. The criterion's scope therefore excludes these links. This is distinct from F73, which fails when a link IS distinguished by colour but lacks a non-colour cue; here the link is not distinguished by colour at all.

cases.aspectTitle: Scoping boundary cases: 3:1-lightness pass, pure-color reliance fails regardless of contrast, non-applicability, and visited-link exemption
cases.scenario: Newsroom investigations archive where article links are underlined (distinguished from static text by a non-colour cue) and visited vs unvisited links differ by colour only, with ~1.09:1 contrast between the two link colours (below 3:1). PASSES via the visited-link exemption.
cases.mechanism: Links are distinguished from static text by an UNDERLINE (no F73 failure on the link-vs-text axis). The only colour-only distinction is visited (purple #5a3da8) vs unvisited (blue #1a52b5) at ~1.09:1, below 3:1. The Understanding note exempts colour-only visited/unvisited distinction even below 3:1, because the :visited pseudo-class is constrained to colour for privacy and conveying visited state is not an author responsibility. Both link colours still meet SC 1.4.3 against the page (~7:1).

cases.aspectTitle: Scoping boundary cases: 3:1-lightness pass, pure-color reliance fails regardless of contrast, non-applicability, and visited-link exemption
cases.scenario: Cinema showtime picker (radio-as-pills) where the chosen showtime is distinguished by inverting the pill's foreground and background (unselected dark-text-on-white; selected white-text-on-dark). The inversion is an additional visual distinction with ~15.7:1 lightness difference, so it PASSES.
cases.mechanism: The selected state reverses the pill's foreground and background colours rather than tinting it. This is not a hue cue: in greyscale the selected pill is a DARK block among LIGHT blocks, differing from the unselected fills by ~15.7:1 in lightness, so it is unmistakable without colour perception. The Understanding note states inversion passes 1.4.1 given sufficient contrast. Selection is also exposed via the native radio's checked state.

cases.aspectTitle: UI buttons, controls, and color-coded categories signalling action/status by color with no text or character cue (G14)
cases.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE: online-tuition 'Confirm enrolment' step with a green button labelled 'Go' (confirm/charge) and a red button labelled 'Cancel' (discard), with instructions naming the labelled buttons. The canonical G14 sufficient pattern; the passing boundary for case-01's failing 'Submit'/'Submit' pair.
cases.mechanism: G14 satisfied: the action conveyed by green/red is redundantly carried by each control's visible programmatic text ('Go' / 'Cancel') and by instructions referencing those labels. In grayscale the actions stay unambiguous from the labels; a screen reader hears 'Go button' / 'Cancel button'. Colour is decorative reinforcement, not the sole carrier.

cases.aspectTitle: UI buttons, controls, and color-coded categories signalling action/status by color with no text or character cue (G14)
cases.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE: light-rail weekend departures TABLE where service tracks are shown by background hue AND every departure carries an in-text '· T1 / · T2 / · T3' code after the destination, with a legend tying each code to its line. The G14 sufficient colour-coded-schedule pattern; the passing boundary for case-04.
cases.mechanism: G14 satisfied: the track category conveyed by tr.t1/.t2/.t3 background hue is redundantly conveyed by the span.code text ('· T1' etc.) in every destination cell. In grayscale the codes remain legible so the track stays distinguishable; a screen reader hears e.g. 'Harbour Int'l Airport · T2'. Colour is redundant reinforcement.

cases.aspectTitle: Arrow-key / roving-tabindex composite-widget traps (menu, grid, listbox, radiogroup, tablist, slider)
cases.scenario: Restaurant online-ordering 'Browse menu' dropdown built as an APG role=menu with roving tabindex; arrows move among dishes but the keydown handler also preventDefault()s Tab/Shift+Tab and remaps them to item movement, so once focus enters the open menu it can never reach the promo field or the checkout button. No Esc, no documented exit.
cases.mechanism: keydown listener on ul[role=menu] has a `case 'Tab': e.preventDefault()` branch that confiscates Tab/Shift+Tab and routes them through the roving-tabindex item mover; arrows are captured legitimately but Tab is also swallowed so focus is confined to the five menuitems with no standard exit and no advised alternate (verified: 6 Tab presses stay on role=menuitem, never reach #promo/#applyBtn).

cases.aspectTitle: Required-input / sequential-gate exception: a section that demands interaction before focus progresses is NOT a failure
cases.scenario: Public-library account-signup form: a required email field suppresses a plain forward Tab while the value is not a valid e-mail (so it LOOKS like a trap), then releases focus to the password field, submit button and rest of the page the instant a valid address is typed by keyboard. Shift+Tab is never blocked. Conformant keyboard-satisfiable input gate (PASS boundary variant).
cases.mechanism: A scoped keydown handler on the required #email input calls preventDefault() on a plain forward Tab only while !checkValidity(); once a valid e-mail is entered by keyboard the gate releases and standard Tab advances. The required interaction is keyboard-completable and focus then progresses, exactly matching the TT Test 2.b Note carve-out, so there is no trap.

cases.aspectTitle: Multi-element region loop: G21 mechanism #1 (Tab must exit the subset after the final location) where no advice is owed
cases.scenario: Coffee-blog article with a 5-link tag cloud between the article body and a 'Keep reading' related-links section. Forward Tab from the last tag correctly exits to the related links, but Shift+Tab on the FIRST tag is intercepted and jumps to the last tag — a one-directional (reverse-only) loop. The judge must test BOTH directions to find it; no advice.
cases.mechanism: G21 mechanism #1 holds forward but is VIOLATED backward: forward Tab from the last tag exits to the related links (#relFirst), yet Shift+Tab from the first tag wraps to the last tag, cycling among the five tags so the article and header above are unreachable from within the region. Plain Shift+Tab is a standard exit method so no advice is owed; the page fails because one direction of the region boundary does not let Tab cross.

cases.aspectTitle: Focus order interleaves between two semantically distinct sections/groups (the canonical Understanding form failure)
cases.scenario: ATS job application (Talentforge) Background step, single-column layout with two stacked sections — Education (Highest degree, School/university, Graduation year) wholly above Work experience (Most recent job title, Most recent company, Years in role). The DOM interleaves the two sections row-by-row (education-degree, work-title, education-school, work-company, ...) and CSS grid pins each field into its section block, so with no tabindex keyboard focus jumps ~300px down to Work and back up to Education on alternate Tabs while a sighted user sees two clean stacked blocks.
cases.mechanism: Two semantic groups (Education vs. Work experience) are interleaved by raw DOM order in a single-column layout, so focus alternates between the two CV sections instead of completing each. The applicant starts describing their degree, is yanked down past the 'Work experience' heading into their job history, then back up to their school — the two distinct parts of a résumé are woven together, making it easy to type a university into the company field or a job title where the degree belongs.

cases.aspectTitle: A specific, well-formed link name that contradicts its actual on-page destination (deceptive but descriptive name)
cases.scenario: PASS control: a healthcare patient-portal information hub with the SAME structure as the failing cases (skip link, in-page jump list, footer document links, labelled #fragment sections) but where every descriptive name correctly matches its destination: 'Read our Privacy Policy'→#privacy (the Privacy Policy), 'Skip to your message inbox'→#inbox, 'Jump to: Booking a flu vaccine'→#flu, 'Read our Notice of Patient Rights'→#rights.
cases.mechanism: Each link's accessible name resolves to the on-page section whose heading matches that name (e.g. 'Read our Privacy Policy'→#privacy headed 'Privacy Policy'), so the name reliably describes the link's actual purpose/destination — the intent of 2.4.4 is met. Exact same-text contrast with case-01 ('Read our Privacy Policy', href '#terms').

cases.aspectTitle: Error text is fluent and field-identifying but factually wrong for the value entered / constraint violated (boilerplate mismatch)
cases.scenario: CONTROL / discrimination foil (PASS). Event-ticketing phone field, post-submit error state — near-identical component to case-01. The retained value is '(202) 555-CALL', which genuinely contains parentheses, a space, a dash, and the letters C-A-L-L. The field is digits-only and the visible associated error reads 'Phone number must contain only digits. Remove the letters, spaces, and parentheses (for example, enter 2025550143).' — a cause that DID occur and correctly describes this value's actual defect.
cases.mechanism: No defect: the described cause matches the entered value's actual error (non-digit characters in a digits-only field) and gives a concrete corrected example, so the user can determine what is wrong and fix it. SC 3.3.1 satisfied. Included to force value-vs-message discrimination rather than a blanket 'phone-digit error = fail' heuristic.

cases.aspectTitle: Error is signalled ONLY by visual styling (red border / colour / icon glyph) with no error meaning in text anywhere on the page
cases.scenario: CONTROL (discrimination boundary): auction 'place a bid' form with the IDENTICAL red border + tint on the email field, but the error is also identified and described in text ('Email address is not valid.') tied via aria-describedby, with aria-invalid='true' and the decorative icon aria-hidden. Should pass.
cases.mechanism: The aria-describedby association surfaces the message and aria-invalid surfaces the state, so a screen reader hears 'Email address, invalid entry, ..., Email address is not valid.' The error is identified and described IN TEXT; the red styling/icon are now acceptable ADDITIONAL cues (icon aria-hidden so it is not double-announced).
